query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the nature of the X element governs the formation of a coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C. Specifically, when X is Al, the alloy promotes an aluminum-rich, high-configurational entropy oxide that bonds strongly to the substrate and significantly retards oxygen diffusion, whereas for X = Si or Mn the resulting oxide is less cohesive and more prone to cracking or spalling.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys in a controlled single-phase or well-characterized multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloys to a high-temperature (≥900 °C) oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Oxidation tests performed at temperatures above 900 °C for an extended period (e.g., 100 hours) under a controlled oxidizing environment.
generation.structural_mediator: A coherent, slow-growing, high-entropy oxide scale that forms at the substrate-oxide interface.
generation.mechanism: The X element modulates the thermodynamics and kinetics of oxide formation. In the case of Al, the formation of an Al-rich oxide with high configurational disorder leads to a dense, adherent scale that impedes oxygen diffusion and minimizes thermal stress-induced cracking. For alloys with Si or Mn, the oxide scale forms with inferior adhesion and faster growth kinetics, making it susceptible to cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Al-containing CrFeCoNiAl alloys will exhibit thinner, homogeneous, and crack-free protective oxide scales with slower growth rates, whereas CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn alloys will display thicker, less coherent oxides that are more prone to cracking or spallation under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: Comparative oxidation performance of CrFeCoNiX alloys with varying X (Al, Si, Mn) prepared under identical processing conditions and in the same initial single-/multiphasic solid-solution state.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys in controlled single-phase or well-defined multiphase states, exposed to oxidative/corrosive environments at temperatures above 900 °C, with minimal extraneous mechanical stresses.
generation.uncertainty: The precise influence of interactions among other alloying elements and possible variations in processing-induced microstructures on oxide scale formation remains to be fully elucidated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples where X is systematically varied (Al, Si, Mn). Subject all samples to oxidation tests at 950 °C in a controlled oxidizing atmosphere for 100 hours. After exposure, perform a series of analyses including measurements of oxide scale thickness (using cross-sectional microscopy), phase composition (via XRD and EDS), and adhesion/cohesion (using scratch tests or thermal cycling).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth rate
Phase composition and elemental distribution in the oxide
Adhesion/cohesion quality of the oxide scale
Presence of cracks or spallation via SEM/TEM analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not form a significantly thinner, more coherent, and adherent oxide layer compared to the Si or Mn variants, or if no clear differences in oxygen diffusion rates and oxide stability are observed, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Various stability criteria developed for high-entropy alloys are applied to compositions produced by mechanical alloying. While they agree with the annealed samples, these criteria fail to describe the as-milled metastable systems, highlighting the ability of mechanical alloying to overcome the limitations imposed by these criteria. The criteria are based on atomic size (Ω ≥ 1.1 and δr ≤ 6.6%) and/or electronegativity misfit, as well as on mixing enthalpy (Λ>0.95 J mol−1K−1 and −5 kJ mol−1<∆Hmix<0), or purely thermodynamic (ϕYe>20; ϕKing>1; Teff<500 K). These criteria are applied to several compositions found in the literature and to two metastable fcc solid solutions produced by mechanical alloying with compositions Al0.75CoXFeNi with X = Cr and Mn. Single-phase microstructures are stable up to above 600 K, leading to more stable multiphase systems after annealing above this temperature. Mössbauer spectrometry shows that, whereas the alloy with Cr is paramagnetic in the as-milled and annealed state, the alloy with Mn changes from paramagnetic to ferromagnetic behavior (Curie temperature ~700 K) after annealing. For AlCrMnNbTiV and AlCrMoNbTiV 17,830 (3.8%) and 17,289 (3.7%) out of 473,382 compositions sampled were single phase HEAs at 800 K. For AlCrFeTiV and AlCrMnMoTi only 356 (0.041%) and 785 (0.091%) out of 862,750 compositions sampled were single phase HEAs at 800 K. In Figure 6 and Figure 7 on average 64% and 67% of the grid points of the two-dimensional projections for AlCrMnNbTiV and AlCrMoNbTiV have circles on them, while in Figure 4 and Figure 5 these percentages are only 6.8% and 9.4% for AlCrFeTiV and AlCrMnMoTi.
